Recommendations  
 Receive the final draft of the Lawrence Loop - Downtown Preliminary Feasibility Study and 
consider providing a recommendation on the alignment and proceeding with the 
Transportation Alternatives grant. 
  
Executive Summary  
 The City contracted with Trekk Design Group to complete a feasibility study for the Lawrence 
Loop - Downtown project. This study evaluates the preferred potential alignment between 
Constant Park and the Santa Fe Depot, as identified through a public survey as part of the 
update to the Lawrence Bikes Plan. 
  
The study gathered existing conditions information, coordinated with critical stakeholders, 
explored the feasibility of the preferred alignment, identified permitting requirements and 
produced planning-level costs. 
  
For the purposes of the study, the project was broken into three segments. A conceptual 
plan was developed, and each segment was analyzed for geometric constraints, utility 
conflicts, right-of-way impacts and any design exceptions needed. 
  
Through the development of the study and evolving conversations with city management, not 
all of the public's preferred alignment can be completed. Parts of Segments 1a and 2 are not 
feasible to construct given potential development of the City-owned parking garage. With 
potential future development of this property, there may be an opportunity to incorporate 
additional trail improvements. 
  
Given Segment 1a is not feasible, the study also considers Segment 1, which received 40% 
support from the public in the survey. Next, the southern limits of Segment 2 remain feasible, 
but the northern limits on the parking garage property are not, thus making the entirety of 
Segment 2 unfeasible since no connection to New Hampshire Street is available. During the 
site walkthrough, potential was seen for a possible alignment of the trail along New 
Hampshire Street from E 7th Street, given the tight corridor between the parking garage and 
the former Reuter Organ Company building (612 New Hampshire Street). This new 
alignment, which was not discussed in the public survey, was also explored in the study. 
Page 1 of 30
Page 35 of 70
  
The study recommends an alignment along Segment 1, Segment 2 Alternative and Segment 
3 (south City Hall connection). 
  
The project has been awarded $1.23 million through a federal Transportation Alternatives 
grant administered through the Kansas Department of Transportation. An agreement for this 
grant is anticipated at the end of this year and will be brought before the City Commission for 
approval. A recommendation from the Connected City Advisory Board will be included in the 
agenda item for the City Commission's consideration.

PR5-B23003 Lawrence Loop Downtown – Preliminary Feasibility Study – Constant Park to 7 th & New York Street 2 
Introduction 
The City of Lawrence, Kansas, in coordination with TREKK Design Group, is conducting a Preliminary 
Feasibility Study to evaluate potential alignments for completing a critical gap in the Lawrence Loop trail 
system through downtown Lawrence. The study area generally extends from Constant Park to the 7th Street 
and New York Street intersection. Previous public engagement identified Segments 1 or 1a, 2a, and 3a as 
the preferred path alternatives, which were evaluated further as part of this study. Figure 1 shows all of 
the alignments that were presented to the public for feedback. 
 
Figure 1: Project Limits Study Area 
Project Need 
The Lawrence Loop is a series of connected trails that, when completed, will provide a continuous urban 
greenway over 22 miles long around the City of Lawrence. The loop is an important part of Lawrence’s 
unmistakable identity and provides residents and visitors alike, a safe and secure way to experience 
Lawrence by walking, wheeling, or biking. There are currently only three segments that still need completed, 
one of which will be completed with this project. 
Project Purpose 
The purpose of this Preliminary Feasibility Study is to identify a feasible and preferred loop alignment that 
provides continuous connectivity through the downtown core. The study will assess alignment feasibility, 
constructability, permitting requirements, stakeholder considerations, and planning-level project costs. 
Recommendations will support future design and funding applications while advancing the City’s goal of 
providing a safe, comfortable, and accessible facility for pedestrians and bicyclists. 
Project Background 
Through previous planning efforts and public engagement, the City has identified a general preference 
for a downtown Lawrence connection using a trail separated from vehicular traffic where practical. Key 
stakeholders will be engaged early in the process as part of this project to consider potential constraints 
and feasibility options. These stakeholders include BNSF Railway, Evergy, and the Kansas Department of 
Transportation (KDOT). The resulting feasibility study will establish a clear path forward for closing the 
downtown gap in the Lawrence Loop and create a more connected active transportation network for the 
Lawrence community.

PR5-B23003 Lawrence Loop Downtown – Preliminary Feasibility Study – Constant Park to 7 th & New York Street 3 
Existing Conditions 
The project study area as shown in Figure 2 traverses a diverse urban terrain containing existing roadway 
corridors as well as undeveloped open space that may provide opportunities for shared-use path 
construction. Land uses vary throughout the area including open space near Constant Park and Robinson 
Park on the west side, mixed corridor use near City Hall, and a mix of Civic and Institutional, Downtown 
Commercial, Residential, and General Industrial eastward to the Amtrak Depot. Physical constraints include 
steep retaining terrain, heavily wooded areas, existing access walls, private utilities, vehicular 
drives/crossings, parking, and right-of-way considerations. Existing conditions vary considerably between 
segments, with each section presenting unique opportunities and challenges related to trail user comfort, 
constructability, right-of-way availability, stakeholder considerations, and connectivity. 
 
Figure 2: Existing Conditions - Project Location Map 
As part of this study, representatives from the City of Lawrence and TREKK conducted a site walk to review 
existing conditions and document key findings and photos. The following sections summarize the key 
characteristics, constraints, and opportunities identified in each study segment, presented from west to east. 
 
 
Page 5 of 30
Page 39 of 70
 
 
 
 
PR5-B23003 Lawrence Loop Downtown – Preliminary Feasibility Study – Constant Park to 7 th & New York Street 4 
Segment 3 Western Limits (Adjacent to Evergy Substation and US-59 Bridges) 
The portion of Segment 3 that spans from the western limits of the study area to City Hall has some of the 
most significant constraints within the study area. These include BNSF right-of-way impacts, Kansas 
Department of Transportation (KDOT) considerations near US-59 bridges, and a nearby Evergy substation.  
Preliminary discussions with Evergy indicated the green space between the roadway and substation may 
accommodate a shared-use path. The existing berm and native trees provide screening for the substation 
and should remain where practical. Signalized pedestrian crossings exist along north 6th Street at the US-
59 intersections, but they are limited to sidewalk width and are less desirable for shared-use path users 
due to heavy traffic and conflict exposure. The separated US-59 bridges are 40-mph principal arterials, 
while 6th Street is a 35-mph principal arterial carrying nearly 23,000 vehicles per day. 
KDOT and BNSF discussions indicated that a shared-use path beneath the bridges, within existing BNSF 
right-of-way, may be feasible, provided the bridge abutments remain undisturbed. BNSF indicated it may 
be open to the City acquiring BNSF right-of-way where the railroad right-of-way width exceeds 40 feet. 
Because BNSF requires a minimum 40-foot corridor through this area, as shown in Figure 3, the additional 
width beneath the bridges is less critical to railroad operations and may be used for City improvements. 
Safety rail and other requirements, such as anti-throw fencing, may be needed on both sides of the path 
as agency agreements are finalized while also maintaining at least 8 feet of vertical clearance beneath 
the existing bridge girders. The area beneath the bridges slopes steeply toward the BNSF railroad and is 
within the FEMA Zone AE floodplain, which may require further analysis during design.

Segment 3 Eastern Limits (Adjacent to City Hall) 
The portion of Segment 3 that spans from the US-59 bridges through the City Hall property to the parking 
garage entrance(s) consists primarily of green space with steep grades and established civic uses. The more 
than 10-foot elevation change across the City Hall site creates slopes over 15%, presenting grading 
challenges for a shared-use path. An existing 11-foot-wide access road serves a few parking spaces and 
solid waste services behind City Hall. Alignment options through this area will require further evaluation of 
grading impacts, accessibility, and user experience as summarized in a later section of this study. 
The westbound to northbound right-turn lane for northbound US-59 extends along 6 th Street and around 
the horizontal curve where 6 th Street transitions to New Hampshire Street, exceeding 400’ in length. The 
site walk team identified that this turn lane length could potentially be reduced to provide more space 
beyond the roadway curb for the shared-use path and reconfiguration of the parking garage accesses. 
New Hampshire Street and 6th Street are identified as collector roadways with a posted speed limit of 20 
mph and serve nearly 11,000 vehicles per day. There is an existing bus stop between the two parking 
garage access points, which may be impacted.

Segment 2a (Rhode Island Street & Adjacent to Parking Garage) 
The area adjacent to the existing parking garage provides a key transition area between the western and 
eastern portions of the study area. Existing conditions include open green space with moderate grades as 
well as corridors adjacent to roadways, parking land uses, and private property. Between the 
redevelopment areas on the west and the existing parking garage on the east/north are moderate slopes 
with a shallow drainage swale. There is existing sidewalk on both sides of Rhode Island Street, some of 
which is brick, with steep grades down to the roadway curbs. Providing a shared-use path on the west side 
of Rhode Island Street may allow for more standard crossing locations and reduce impacts to other existing 
characteristics such as mature trees.  
 
Segment 2b/c (Adjacent to New Hampshire Street and 7th Street) 
Segment 2b and 2c generally follows New Hampshire Street to the south and 7 th Street to the east. The 
existing pedestrian facilities on the east side of New Hampshire Street consist of 5’ sidewalk adjacent to 
existing building frontages. There are existing infrastructure above ground within the greenspace that may 
be impacted such as parking meters, light poles, and other private utilities. Compared to Segment 2a, this 
alignment has less separation from vehicular traffic but may have fewer drainage, grading, and retaining 
wall constraints. 
The intersection of 7th Street with New Hampshire Street and 6th Street from the parking garage entrances 
to the west, including the US-59 bridges, are on the City’s High Injury Network (HIN). New Hampshire Street 
south of the parking garage entrance and 7 th Street between New Hampshire Street and Rhode Island 
Street are included in the City’s Vulnerable Road User (VRU) HIN. These locations should be considered 
during design, as providing safer and more accessible facilities may improve safety of VRU activity in these 
areas.

Segment 1a (Adjacent to BNSF Railroad) 
Segment 1a extends from the existing parking garage near Rhode Island Street to New York Street along 
BNSF right-of-way. The corridor traverses heavily wooded terrain with steep slopes and is located adjacent 
to the BNSF railroad. BNSF indicated that it would be unfeasible to encroach into right-of-way due to the 
existing limited width. Additionally, significant elevation differences exist between the proposed corridor 
and the railroad, with some areas exceeding 30 feet. As a result, walls and fencing would be required 
along this alignment, impacting private properties and necessitating the removal of a significant number of 
existing trees. The property east of New York Street, owned by the Amtrak Depot, would be critical to 
establishing the shared-use path connection. 
Given the topographic and right-of-way constraints, Segment 1a was determined to be infeasible for 
the shared-use path alignment. Further details are shown in the Key Considerations section of this study. 
 
Segment 1 (Adjacent to 7th Street) 
Segment 1 generally follows 7 th Street, a collector roadway, which has a posted speed limit of 25 mph 
serving less than 2,500 vehicles per day. The existing pedestrian facilities on the north side primarily consist 
of 4’ sidewalk, some of which is brick. The existing roadway width is wider than required, providing 
opportunity to reduce travel lane widths and construct curb improvements to provide more favorable 
separation for shared-use path users. Compared to Segment 1a, this alignment has fewer topographic 
challenges, but places users closer to vehicular traffic and has potential conflicts with above ground utilities.

Design Criteria 
The shared-use path will be designed to meet the following design criteria according to AASHTO Guide 
for the Development of Bicycle Facilities – 5th Edition: 
 Material: 6” reinforced concrete (City standard) 
 Width: 10’ min. (Section 6.4.3) 
 Shoulders: 2’ min. at 6:1 max. slope; 5’ desirable (clear of all obstructions) (Section 6.6.1.1) 
 Shy Distance: 1’ min.; 3’ desirable (adjacent to continuous vertical elements) (Section 6.6.1.3) 
 Cross Slope: 1.0% min.; 2% max. (PROWAG) 
 Design Speed: 15 mph (Section 6.5 considering urban, higher volume path with pedestrians) 
 Profile Grade: 0.5% min.; 5% max. (Section 6.6.4.1) 
 Horizontal Curves: 47’ (Section 6.6.3.1 considering 20-degree lean angle at 16 mph design speed)  
o Note that radii as small as 5’ to 15’ may be used at intersections or constrained locations 
 Vertical Curves: Refer to Table 5-2 for SSD based on speed and grade for 2.5-second perception-
reaction time and Table 6-8 for minimum length of crest curve based on SSD (Section 6.6.4.2) 
 Vertical Clearance: 8’ minimum; 10’ desirable (Section 6.6.1.2) 
 Barriers Near Hazardous Conditions:  Where shoulder is less than 5’ in width, a physical barrier, 
railing, or fencing is recommended where: 
o Slopes 3:1 or steeper, with a drop of 6’ or greater, or adjacent to a parallel body of water 
or other substantial obstacle, 
o Slopes 2:1 or steeper, with a drop of 4’ or greater, or 
o Slopes 1:1 or steeper, with a drop of 1’ or greater. (Section 6.6.7) 
The shared-use path will be designed to utilize existing enclosed storm sewer systems where possible. If 
ditches are necessary to maintain existing drainage patterns, then the ditch geometry will generally follow 
the typical section geometry as identified in Figure 4.

Conceptual Design Considerations & Recommendations 
Based on the findings during the site walk and preliminary input from Evergy, KDOT, and BNSF, key 
segments were analyzed further as identified in Figure 5. 
 
Figure 5: Conceptual Design Considerations – Project Location Map 
A conceptual design plan, including analyzed alignments and profiles, was developed as shown in 
Appendix A. The following sections summarize the proposed geometrics highlighting the constraints at key 
locations as well as listing any design exceptions, right-of-way impacts, and utility impacts. 
Key Considerations 
Segment 3 Western Limits (Near Evergy Substation) 
On the western edge of the project limits, the shared-use path may be installed in place of the existing 
sidewalk within the available greenspace separated from 6 th Street. There is sufficient space to install the 
shared-use path in front of the existing traffic signal cabinet at 6 th Street and US-59 south, limiting the 
impact to the existing tree berm, which is acting as a natural screen to the substation behind it. 
As the shared-use path turns northward, it is proposed to separate from US-59 and weave between the 
existing trees, allowing the path to descend and provide sufficient clearance for a crossing beneath the 
US-59 bridge. Due to grading constraints, limited horizontal radii, and the location of the US-59 bridge 
abutments, the proposed path construction limits extend near the existing overhead power pole, which is 
anticipated to remain in place. 
Segment 3 Central Limits (Beneath US-59 Bridges, Adjacent to BNSF) 
The shared-use path has been aligned to provide a minimum 8 foot of vertical clearance to the bottom of 
the existing US-59 girders. Mechanically Stabilized Earth (MSE) fill walls will be necessary on the north 
side of the path and Integral Sidewalk Retaining Walls (ISRW) will be necessary in the cut section on the 
south side. Fencing should separate the path from the bridges to limit pedestrian activity beneath them, 
and safety rail should protect users from fall hazards. Final details should be coordinated through agency 
agreements.

Segment 3 Eastern Limits (Adjacent to City Hall) 
East of the US-59 bridges, the path could route around City Hall either to the north or south, or both if 
desired to create a loop around City Hall. 
South of City Hall Connection Alternative 
Providing a connection on the south side of City Hall requires a grade of nearly 13% to get the shared-
use path back up to the grade of 6 th Street from beneath the US-59 bridges. Additionally, the horizontal 
curve is smaller than required by design criteria and vertical curve constraints result in reduced stopping 
sight distances. The combination of the horizontal and vertical conditions as compared to the design criteria 
could become challenging to safely navigate. 
North of City Hall Connection Alternative 
On the north side of City Hall is flat terrain with historic silos acting as retaining walls on the north side. It 
is proposed to place the trail within this shallow drainage swale and accommodate the existing drainage 
patterns with shallow ditches on either side with pipes crossing the trail or a series of trench drains. It is 
proposed to fill in the existing swale by about a foot to provide necessary clearances for drainage pipes 
and to limit the slope up to the existing grade at 6th Street. 
The shared-use path is proposed to be routed through the existing greenspace versus adjacent to the 
existing parking garage access to limit the combination of steep slopes and tight horizontal curves. The 
required slope to return to grade at 6th Street exceeds 15% and vertical curve constraints result in reduced 
stopping sight distances. 
With the north path option, the existing service road/parking would be impacted behind City Hall. 
However, a portion of the service road could likely remain in service for trash pickup and other services. 
The combination of the drainage and vertical constraints as compared to the design criteria could become 
challenging to mitigate. However, routing the path adjacent to the river could activate the space and 
provide further opportunity for overlook areas to adjacent scenery. 
Segment 2a Northern Limits (Adjacent to Parking Garage) 
Due to the existing locations of the parking garage structural signage, the shared-use path will need to use 
the space of the existing bus pull-out along 6th Street. Buses can be accommodated with in-lane passenger 
loading in the outside lane of 6th Street, as the lane functions as a dedicated right-turn lane with more than 
400 feet of storage length. 
As the path turns eastward on the south side of the existing parking garage, there may be some 
encroachment onto private property, which should be further coordinated with the property owner. The 
City has already been in contact with this property owner. The shared-use path may be aligned adjacent 
to the parking garage barriers with sufficient shy distance. As this area is an existing shallow drainage 
swale, the existing drainage patterns should be accommodated with either a shallow ditch on the south and 
west side of the trail or with a series of trench drains. 
As the path extends beyond the southern edge of the parking garage, the existing surface parking lot is 
anticipated to be impacted due to the limited amount of green space between the parking lot and the 
parking garage. As the concept shows in Appendix A, six parking spaces are expected to be lost due to 
the implementation of the shared-use path in this area. The path may be adjacent to the artwork, providing 
a positive experience to Loop users. 
However, after this alignment was assessed for feasibility, direction from City Management indicated that 
no shared-use path should be pursued on the One Riverfront Plaza Parking property due to potential future 
development. An alignment along the New Hampshire Street frontage may still be viable as summarized 
in a subsequent section of this study.

Segment 2a Southern Limits (Adjacent to Rhode Island Street) 
Providing the shared-use path along the west side of Rhode Island Street provides a standard north/south 
crossing of the parking lot entrance and allows for the Rhode Island Street crossing to be at the intersection 
of 7th Street. The alignment takes advantage of the existing green space between the curb and right-of-
way. The existing steep grade of this area will require an ISRW on the west side of the proposed path to 
tie-into existing grades. 
Given that the alignment through the One Riverfront Plaza Parking property has been deemed unfeasible, 
this segment will have no option to continue to the north and cannot be considered. 
Segment 2b/c (Adjacent to New Hampshire Street & 7th Street) 
An alternate alignment identified during the site walk could route Segment 2 along New Hampshire Street 
and 7th Street, as shown in Appendix A, rather than adjacent to the existing parking garage and along 
Rhode Island Street. Much of this alignment can be accommodated within the existing greenspace adjacent 
to the roadway, minimizing impacts to existing on-street parking. However, the back of the proposed path 
approaches the existing right-of-way limits, which generally coincides with adjacent building frontages. 
Several overhead utilities may require coordination or relocation as part of this alternative. Consideration 
for maintaining parking adjacent to the shared-use path should also be considered, such as appropriate 
buffers for vehicular doors and mixed uses. 
While this option provides less separation from vehicular traffic, it may have fewer drainage, grading, 
and retaining wall constraints. This option also avoids encroachment onto the One Riverfront Plaza Parking 
property. New Hampshire Street south of the parking garage entrance and 7 th Street between New 
Hampshire Street and Rhode Island Street are included in the City’s Vulnerable Road User (VRU) HIN. These 
locations should be considered during design, as providing safer and more accessible facilities may improve 
safety of VRU activity in these areas as issues are studied and addressed appropriately. 
Segment 1a (Adjacent to BNSF) 
The preferred alignment, as identified through public engagement, for Segment 1 is along BNSF right-of-
way from the existing parking garage near Rhode Island Street to New York Street. This corridor is heavily 
wooded terrain with steep slopes, which would require retaining walls on each side with some portions of 
the wall being up to 8’ in height. As shown in Appendix A, there are significant impacts to private properties 
at the following locations: 
 624 Rhode Island Street 
 620 Rhode Island Street 
 600 Rhode Island Street 
 621 Connecticut Street 
 630 Connecticut Street 
 633 New York Street 
 646 Connecticut Street 
GIS property lines indicate the alignment may also affect BNSF property. However, the necessary area 
could potentially be acquired if a 40-foot railroad right-of-way is maintained, consistent with adjacent 
right-of-way width. In addition to substantial private property impacts, some existing structures such as 
garages or sheds may also be affected. Routing the Loop through this segment would approximately 
double the project required retaining wall area, significantly increasing construction costs. If this alternative 
is pursued, an improved crossing should be considered near the existing railroad signal arm at New York 
Street. 
As is the case with Segment 2 Northern Limits (Adjacent to the Parking Garage), this alignment was 
determined to be unfeasible due to potential future development of the One Riverfront Plaza Parking 
property.

Segment 1 (Adjacent to 7th Street)

where the improvements encroach onto private property, which should be considered as design and 
construction progresses. Below are the identified right-of-way impacts for the recommended loop alignment  
(Segment 3, Segment 2b/c, and Segment 1): 
 BNSF Right-of-Way Beneath US-59 Bridges (Segment 3 Central Limits) 
o Coordination with BNSF confirmed that the City may be able to encroach on existing BNSF 
property, provided a minimum 40-foot BNSF right-of-way width is maintained. 
As design advances, temporary construction easements may be needed where grading limits approach 
adjacent properties. Permanent wall and drainage easements should also be considered for long-term 
maintenance.

Private Utility Impacts 
As part of the conceptual design survey, utilities were marked through Kansas One-Call and field-collected. 
Based on those markings, this section identifies potential conflicts for further review during design. In some 
areas, the proposed shared-use path would be constructed over existing buried gas or fiber optic facilities, 
which may not conflict depending on utility depth. Several existing drainage grates will need to be 
addressed with the proposed drainage improvements, and multiple water valves and utility manholes 
should be adjusted to grade. Specific impacts for the recommended loop alignment  (Segment 3, Segment 
2b/c, and Segment 1) are listed below. 
Near Evergy Substation, US-59 Bridges/BNSF, and City Hall (Segment 3) 
 The existing overhead power pole between Evergy’s substation and the southbound US-59 bridge 
may avoid direct impacts. However, if conflicts are unavoidable, relocation efforts are expected 
to be significant. 
 There are existing manholes on the east side of the substation that may need adjusted as these 
feed underground power. 
 There is overhead power that transitions to underground between the US-59 bridges that should 
be considered during design as it appears that construction may be working within the vicinity of 
this infrastructure. 
Adjacent to New Hampshire Street & 7th Street (Segment 2b/c) 
 The existing light poles on the east side of New Hampshire Street will be impacted and should be 
considered. 
 The existing parking meters should be considered as they may constrain the pedestrian walkway 
width between the building frontages if replaced. 
Adjacent to 7th Street (Segment 1) 
 Evergy-owned overhead power poles along 7th Street will be impacted and may need to be 
relocated within the expanded greenspace. Evergy noted that some relocations may be difficult 
because overhead lines extend in all four directions.

Conclusion & Recommendations 
Based on existing conditions, stakeholder input, design criteria, conceptual alignment options, and potential 
future development considerations, this study found that the downtown gap in the Lawrence Loop can be 
closed with a feasible connection along segments 3, 2b/c, and 1, provided the required design exceptions 
are approved. 
The recommended alignment generally uses existing greenspace along 6th Street, routes around the Evergy 
property, and continues beneath the US-59 bridges. The primary unresolved decision is whether the path 
should pass north or south of City Hall, as both options present constraints. The north connection includes 
drainage challenges within the existing swale and steep grades, while the south connection includes tight 
curves and steep grades. Recommendation is given to the south alignment because of the opportunity to 
provide a more direct connection to downtown. 
East of City Hall, the path cannot continue adjacent to the parking garage, within the One Riverfront Plaza 
Parking property, due to potential future development. An alternate route along New Hampshire Street 
and 7th Street has been considered that would place the path closer to traffic and may affect parking, 
which may not align with public input to date. 
The list below further summarizes the feasibility constraints for each segment identified herein. 
 Segment 3 Western Limits (Near Evergy Substation) 
o Feasibility requires a profile design exception. 
 Segment 3 Central Limits (Beneath US-59 Bridges, Adjacent to BNSF) 
o Feasibility requires right-of-way acquisition, retaining walls, safety rail, and fencing. 
 Segment 3 Eastern Limits (Adjacent to City Hall) 
o South of City Hall Connection 
 Feasibility requires alignment and profile design exceptions. 
o North of City Hall Connection 
 Feasibility requires a profile design exception with additional considerations for 
drainage improvements. 
 Segment 2 Northern Limits (Adjacent to Parking Garage) 
o Unfeasible due to encroachment onto One Riverfront Plaza Parking property. 
 Segment 2 Southern Limits (Adjacent to Rhode Island Street) 
o Unfeasible as alignment requires dependency on Northern Limits, which is unfeasible. 
 Segment 1a (Adjacent to BNSF) 
o Unfeasible due to encroachment onto One Riverfront Plaza Parking property. Segment 1a 
would significantly increase construction costs given the topographic challenges and right-
of-way constraints. 
 Segment 1 (Adjacent to 7th Street) 
o Feasibility requires roadway curb improvements and overhead utility relocations. 
The estimated construction cost is approximately $1.8M. Advancing the project into preliminary design 
should focus on further evaluating the remaining alternatives, refining grading and drainage solutions, and 
confirming the alignment(s) that best balances user experience, constructability, right-of-way impacts, and 
cost.

Other Design Considerations & Next Steps 
The next step before construction and implementation of the proposed improvements includes securing 
funding and developing construction plans during a design phase. Design should adhere to the 
recommendations summarized, however further details should be developed including, but not limited to, 
the following: 
 Detailed analysis and design of storm sewer improvements. 
 Evaluation and design of sidewalk ramps per ADA compliance requirements and conditions. 
 Determination of safety railing extents and other safety barrier considerations. 
 Structural analysis and design of retaining wall improvements. 
 Considerations for lighting improvements. 
 Continued coordination with BNSF, KDOT, and Evergy. 
 Evaluate crash history of HIN locations to provide recommendations for safety improvements. 
o New Hampshire Street, 6 th Street, and 7 th Street are all on the HIN or the VRU HIN. 
Improving road user safety for all users will be a key design criteria as this project moves 
forward in design. 
 Considerations for additional public input/engagement, building upon engagement that was 
facilitated as part of the Lawrence Bikes Plan 2026 update. 
o The Lawrence Bikes Plan update provided recommended routing for the Lawrence Loop 
through Downtown. 
 Considerations for connections to North Lawrence as identified in North Lawrence Corridor Study 
(NLCS). 
o The NLCS study considered connections from North Lawrence to the downtown area but 
does not influence and did not consider the routing of the Lawrence Loop. 
 Considerations for Riverfront redevelopment opportunities. 
o The City recently, in 2026, acquired the Riverfront property. Any future demolitions or 
developments could connect to the recommended Loop alignment in this study. The Loop 
connection proposed in this feasibility study would still be applicable and useable if the 
Riverfront is redeveloped. This proposed connection would still provide routes for multimodal 
users to get from downtown to any future developments. 
 Considerations for appropriate pavement markings and symbols to connect to other adjacent bike 
networks such as at 6th Street and Mass Street as well as 6th Street and Vermont Street. 
 Considerations for VRU improvements at 7 th Street and New Hampshire Street such as raised 
crosswalks or a raised intersection.
